To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the controlling mechanism of SOA formation is the rate of gas-phase oxidation and that SOA formation is enhanced in the presence of pre-existing organic mass, but only if the pre-existing organic aerosols are reactive.
the rate of formation of secondary particulate organic matter (POM) is determined by the rate of oxidation of the parent hydrocarbons and the rate of gas-particle partitioning.

the SOA yield is determined by the rate of parent-hydrocarbon oxidation and the extent of oxidation of first-generation species, but is insensitive to the rate of gas-phase reaction of the first-generation species and the extent of reaction and rate of parent hydrocarbons.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the mechanisms that control secondary organic aerosol formation in the atmosphere.
the formation of secondary organic particulate matter (SOPM) in the atmosphere.
the development of a comprehensive model for the formation of SOA from the reaction of volatile organic compounds (VOC) in the presence of NO _{x}.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the mechanisms controlling SOA formation are not well constrained by laboratory chamber data alone.
, in the absence of detailed chemical measurements, it is difficult to infer the mechanisms controlling SOA formation from chamber data alone.

SOA formation can result from a variety of mechanisms, including partitioning of parent hydrocarbon, gas-phase reactions of parent hydrocarbon and/or its oxidation products, and gas-phase reactions that produce more or less volatile products.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
SOA formation is most sensitive to particle-phase reaction and to the extent of reaction, and least sensitive to the rate of parent oxidation.
SOA formation mechanisms can be inferred from chamber data, but only when the data set is comprehensive and includes direct measurements of key species.
SOA formation mechanisms can be determined from laboratory experiments, but the interpretation of the data is complicated by a number of factors.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the mechanisms controlling SOA formation are not necessarily evident from chamber experiments, even those that are well characterized.

the mechanisms of SOA yield and formation rate cannot be inferred from chamber measurements of the SOA yield alone; additional data are needed to determine whether the SOA yield is limited by the partitioning of parent hydrocarbon or by the rate of parent oxidation, and whether the SOA formation rate is controlled by gas-phase or particle-phase chemistry.

the controlling mechanisms of particle-phase chemistry can be inferred from chamber data only when both the particle-phase reaction rate constant and the particle-phase reaction order can be independently determined.
